title: Why the prophets spoke in riddles
source_text: Ἐχρῆν δὲ αὐτὸν, εἴπερ εὐγνωμόνει πρὸς τὴν κατηγορίαν, ἐκθέσθαι αὐταῖς λέξεσι τὰς προφητείας, εἴτ᾿ ἐν αἷς θεὸς παντοκράτωρ ἐπηγγέλλετο εἶναι ὁ λέγων, εἴτ᾿ ἐν αἷς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, εἴτε καὶ ἐν αἷς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον λέγον εἶναι ἐπιστεύετο· οὕτω γὰρ καὶ ἠγωνίασεν ἀνασκευάσαι τὰ εἰρημένα καὶ δεῖξαι ὅτι οὐκ ἔνθεοι ἦσαν οἱ λόγοι, περιέχοντες ἐπιστροφὴν ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων καὶ ἔλεγχον τῶν ποτε ὄντων καὶ πρόγνωσιν περὶ τῶν μελλόντων. διὸ καὶ οἱ κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς ἀπογραψάμενοι τὰς προφητείας αὐτῶν ἐφύλαξαν, ἵνα καὶ οἱ μεταγενέστεροι ἀναγινώσκοντες θαυμάζωσιν ὡς λόγους θεοῦ καὶ ὠφελούμενοι οὐ μόνον ἀπὸ τῶν ἐπιπληκτικῶν καὶ ἐπιστρεπτικῶν ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν προγνωστικῶν ταῖς ἐκβάσεσι πειθόμενοι περὶ τοῦ θεῖον εἶναι πνεῦμα τὸ προειρηκὸς τὴν κατὰ τὸν λόγον εὐσέβειαν ἀσκοῦντες διατελῶσι, πειθόμενοι τῷ νόμῳ καὶ τοῖς προφήταις. οἱ μὲν ουν προφῆται ὅσα ἦν αὐτόθεν νοηθῆναι τοῖς ἀκούουσι χρήσιμα καὶ συμβαλλόμενα τῇ τῶν ἠθῶν ἐπανορθώσει χωρὶς πάσης ἐπικρύψεως κατὰ τὸ βούλημα τοῦ θεοῦ εἰρήκασιν, ὅσα δὲ μυστικώτερα ἦν καὶ ἐποπτικώτερα καὶ ἐχόμενα θεωρίας τῆς ὑπὲρ τὴν πάνδημον ἀκοὴν, ταῦτα „δι᾿ αἰνιγμάτων“ καὶ ἀλληγοριῶν καὶ τῶν καλουμένων σκοτεινῶν λόγων καὶ τῶν ὀνομαζομένων παραβολῶν ἢ παροιμιῶν ἀπεφήναντο· ἵν᾿ οἱ μὴ φυγοπονοῦντες ἀλλὰ πάντα πόνον ὑπὲρ ἀρετῆς καὶ ἀληθείας ἀναδεχόμενοι ἐξετάσαντες εὕρωσι καὶ εὑρόντες, ὡς λόγος αἱρεῖ, οἰκονομήσωσιν. ὁ δὲ γεννάδας Κέλσος ὡσπερεὶ θυμωθεὶς ἐπὶ τῷ μὴ νενοηκέναι τοὺς τῶν προφητῶν τοιούτους λόγους ἐλοιδόρησεν αὐτοὺς, εἰπὼν ὅτι ταῦτα ἐπανατεινάμενοι προστιθέασιν ἐφεξῆς ἄγνωστα καὶ πάροιστρα καὶ πάντῃ ἄδηλα, ὧν τὸ μὲν γνῶμα οὐδεὶς ἂν νοῦν ἔχων εὑρεῖν δύναιτο· ἀσαφῆ γὰρ καὶ τὸ μηδὲν, ἀνοήτῳ δὲ ἢ γόητι παντὶ περὶ παντὸς ἀφορμὴν ἐνδίδωσιν, ὅπῃ βούλεται, τὸ λεχθὲν σφετερίζεσθαι. καὶ πανούργως μοι ἔδοξε ταῦτ᾿ εἰρηκέναι, κωλύειν τὸ ὅσον ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτῷ βουλόμενος τοὺς ἐντυγχάνοντας ταῖς προφητείαις βασανίζειν καὶ ἐξετάζειν αὐτῶν τὸν νοῦν· καὶ πέπονθέ τι πρᾶγμα παραπλήσιον τοῖς εἰποῦσι περί τινος προφήτου, εἰσελθόντος πρός τινα καὶ τὰ μέλλοντα προειπόντος αὐτῷ· „τί εἰσῆλθεν ὁ ἐπίληπτος οὗτος πρός σε;“
pass_a_gloss: He ought (χρή), if he were fair-minded (εὐγνωμονέω) toward the accusation (κατηγορία), to set out (ἐκτίθημι) in the very words (λέξις) the prophecies, whether those in which the one speaking professed (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) to be God almighty (θεὸς παντοκράτωρ), or those in which the Son of God (υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ), or also those in which the Holy Spirit (πνεῦμα ἅγιον) was believed (πιστεύω) to be the one speaking; for so he would also have contended (ἀγωνιάω) to refute (ἀνασκευάζω) the things said and to show that the words were not inspired (ἔνθεος), containing a turning (ἐπιστροφή) from sins (ἁμάρτημα), a reproof (ἔλεγχος) of those then existing, and foreknowledge (πρόγνωσις) about things to come. Therefore those of their time, having written down (ἀπογράφω) their prophecies, preserved (φυλάσσω) them, so that later-born (μεταγενέστερος) also, reading, might marvel (θαυμάζω) as at words of God, and being benefited (ὠφελέω) not only by the rebuking (ἐπιπληκτικός) and converting (ἐπιστρεπτικός) things but also by the predictive (προγνωστικός), persuaded by the outcomes (ἔκβασις) that the Spirit that foretold is divine, might continue (διατελέω) practising (ἀσκέω) the piety (εὐσέβεια) according to the word (λόγος), obeying the law and the prophets. The prophets, then, whatever was useful for hearers to be understood directly (αὐτόθεν) and contributing (συμβάλλομαι) to the correction (ἐπανόρθωσις) of morals (ἦθος), without all concealment (ἐπίκρυψις) according to the will (βούλημα) of God have spoken; but whatever was more mystical (μυστικός) and more epoptic (ἐποπτικός) and holding to contemplation (θεωρία) above the common hearing (πάνδημος ἀκοή), these they declared (ἀποφαίνομαι) 'through riddles' (αἴνιγμα) and allegories (ἀλληγορία) and the so-called dark (σκοτεινός) words and the so-named parables (παραβολή) or proverbs (παροιμία); so that those not fleeing toil (φυγοπονέω) but accepting every toil for virtue (ἀρετή) and truth, having examined (ἐξετάζω), might find, and having found, as reason (λόγος) proves, might manage (οἰκονομέω) [them]. But the noble (γεννάδας, ironic) Celsus, as if enraged (θυμόω) at not having understood such words of the prophets, reviled (λοιδορέω) them, saying [Celsus, repeated from 7.9]: 'Having held these out, they add next unknown, frenzied and wholly unclear things, whose sense no one having mind could find; for they are obscure and nothing, but to every senseless man or sorcerer they give a starting point about anything, in whatever way he wishes, to appropriate what was said.' And he seemed to me to have said these things knavishly (πανούργως), wishing as far as in him lay to prevent (κωλύω) those who read (ἐντυγχάνω) the prophecies from testing (βασανίζω) and examining their sense (νοῦς); and he has suffered something similar to those who said about a certain prophet, who came in to someone and foretold to him the things to come: 'Why did this seized man (ἐπίληπτος) come in to you?'
pass_b_english: But if he had been fair in his accusation, he ought to have set out the prophecies word for word, whether those in which the speaker announced himself to be God almighty, or those in which he announced himself the Son of God, or those in which the speaker was believed to be the Holy Spirit. For then he would have been making a real effort to overturn what was said and to show that the words were not inspired, words that contain a call to turn from sins, a rebuke of the people of that day, and foreknowledge of things to come. That is why those who lived in the prophets’ own time wrote down their prophecies and preserved them: so that later generations too, reading them, might marvel at them as words of God; and, helped not only by the rebukes and calls to conversion but also by the predictions, and convinced by the outcome of events that it was a divine Spirit who had foretold them, might persevere in practising the piety that accords with the word, obeying the law and the prophets.

The prophets, then, in accordance with the will of God, spoke without any concealment whatever their hearers could usefully understand at once and whatever helped to correct their conduct. But what was more mystical, more for the eyes of the initiated, and bound up with a contemplation beyond what the common ear can take in, they set forth “through riddles” (Numbers 12:8), through allegories, through what are called dark sayings, and through what are named parables or proverbs (Proverbs 1:6). They did this so that those who do not shrink from toil, but take on every labour for the sake of virtue and truth, might examine and find, and, having found, might put what they found to use as reason requires.

But the noble Celsus, as though angry at not having understood such words of the prophets, reviled them, saying: “Having brandished all this, they go on to add unintelligible, frenzied and altogether obscure words, whose meaning no one with any sense could discover; for they are unclear and mean nothing, but they give any fool or sorcerer an opening to seize on what was said and make it his own, on any matter and in whatever way he wishes.” He seems to me to have said this with cunning, wishing, so far as lay in his power, to keep readers of the prophecies from testing and examining their meaning. And something has happened to him like what happened to those who said of a certain prophet, who had gone in to someone and foretold the future to him: “Why did this madman come in to you?” (2 Kings 9:11).

choices.choice: Celsus’s sentence is quoted again word for word from 7.9 (Origen writes νοῦν ἔχων for ἔχων νοῦν; same sense) and is in double quotation marks. „δι᾿ αἰνιγμάτων“ is marked as a quotation in the copy-text and matches Numbers 12:8 in the Septuagint (οὐ δι᾿ αἰνιγμάτων, ‘not in riddles’); 1 Corinthians 13:12 (ἐν αἰνίγματι) is a possible secondary echo, not cited inline. The list ‘dark sayings ... parables or proverbs’ alludes to Proverbs 1:6 in the Septuagint (παραβολήν, σκοτεινὸν λόγον, αἰνίγματα); the book title Proverbs is παροιμίαι. The closing quotation is 2 Kings 9:11 (Septuagint 4 Kingdoms 9:11: τί ὅτι εἰσῆλθεν ὁ ἐπίλημπτος οὗτος πρὸς σέ;), said by Jehu’s fellow officers of the young prophet who anointed him; Origen omits ὅτι. ἐπίληπτος (‘seized, frenzied’) rendered ‘madman’. ἔλεγχον τῶν ποτε ὄντων could be masculine (‘a rebuke of the people of that day’, taken here) or neuter (‘an exposure of what then was’). ἐποπτικώτερα, a term from the highest grade of the mysteries, rendered ‘more for the eyes of the initiated’. οὕτω γὰρ καὶ ἠγωνίασεν is an unreal past without ἄν, rendered ‘he would have been making a real effort’ (καί as emphasis). αὐταῖς λέξεσι rendered ‘word for word’. τὴν κατὰ τὸν λόγον εὐσέβειαν rendered ‘the piety that accords with the word’; λόγος may mean the prophetic word or reason. οἰκονομήσωσιν (‘manage, dispense’) rendered ‘put ... to use’. ἐξετάσαντες εὕρωσι may echo Matthew 7:7, but the wording differs; not cited.
αὐταῖς λέξεσι: 'word for word' instead of 'in their own words'
ἠγωνίασεν: 'he would have been making a real effort' instead of 'would at least have striven' ('at least' had no basis in the Greek)
repeated quotation of Celsus made identical to the revised English of 7.9
Scripture checked: Numbers 12:8 (δι᾿ αἰνιγμάτων), Proverbs 1:6 (parable, dark saying, riddles), 2 Kings 9:11 (4 Kingdoms in the Septuagint) confirmed

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
